That it is expedient to provide that when flour or meal is sold or offered for sale by the bag, there shall be plainly stamped or marked on the bag the name of the manufacturer or packer and his address, and the weight of the contents and of the tare of the bag.
He said: Mr. Speaker, chapter 85, section 163, of the Revised Statutes provides that every barrel of flour or meal shall contain 196 pounds, and every half barrel 98 pounds, but there is no provision for selling flour or meal by the bag. In my own county, as [DOT] well as in other counties, I have heard complaints made that millers put up flour, and more particularly corn meal, in bags of different weights. They are supposed to put 98 pounds in a bag, but farmers have told me that when they weighed these bags they found as little as 91 pounds. The House can readily see that the consumer is losing considerable by this method. The amendment I propose to make in the Bill which I shall introduce, if this motion is adopted, is that every manufacturer or packer shall stamp plainly on the bag his name and address, and the weight contained in the bag. The reason that I did not think it would be wise to make a standard weight is that flour, particularly, is sold in half bags, quarter bags, and, I believe, in eighths, and it would be pretty hard to amend any statute so as to provide for conditions of that kind. If the House will allow a Bill for this purpose to be introduced, when it reaches the committee stage, wc will discuss the question more thoroughly.

I see no objection to this resolution, as I understand from the hon. member (Mr. Stanfield)) that it is introduced with the purpose of founding a Bill upon it, and, of course, we will have full opportunity of discussing the details of that Bill. He said : It is reported in the press that the Bill to which this motion has relevance or some similar Bill has been defeated in the Senate of the United States, but I am not clear as to what the exact situation there is. However that may he, it is desirable that we should have all these papers before the House in order that the country may be in a position thoroughly to compre-

'hend the whole situation as it has developed in the United States if ever a similar proposal should be renewed there or in this parliament. I would not care to associate myself with the view which was presented in this House a few days ago. That if the United States did not decrease the level of the water in the River St. Lawrence we have no standing whatever to make a protest against the creation by any corporation formed in that country, of obstructions across the river. I rather regret that the Jdinister of Justice seemed to adopt that view. The channel which has [DOT]been alluded to is one which, under the terms of the Ashburton Treaty, must be free and open forever to the people of both countries. As I understand the argument which was made in this House on the occasion in question, it amounted to this, that if the level of the water is not raised beyond a certain height, the United States can do anything they like in that channel, provided they afford us another channel ; if they establish a private canal, and close the channel up altogether, they are at perfect liberty to do so, and we have absolutely no right, and no standing under international law or otherwise, to make any remonstrance whatever. I would not be inclined to regard the situation in that way. I would consider that we would have a right and a duty to protest if that channel were interfered with by a corporation or by the United States government. They could not possibly be the sole judges as to whether navigation was interfered with or not. They could not possibly arrogate to themselves the sole right to determine whether navigation had been interfered with by the substitution of another channel. Such a statement of the case appears to me an unreasonable one, and I am bound to say that it is not one that I would have expected the government of this country to make through the mouth of the Minister of Justice or through the mouth of any other member of the cabinet. However, that may be, I would think it desirable that the documents alluded to in this motion should be brought down and laid upon the table of the House.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There is no objection whatever to the granting of the motion of my hon. friend. On the contrary, I rather welcome it, and the government will spare no effort to have as complete a record as can be made, so that we shall have before us in due form the exact situation, commencing with the Ashburton Treaty, so that we may ascertain, as far as we can, what our rights in the matter are, and how far they have been complicated or helped by subsequent legislation. Of course, the preparation of such a return will take some time. As to our rights under the Ashburton Treaty, I would
not care to express an opinion at this moment. The Minister of Justice, who is an eminent authority on questions of this kind, apart from his official position, has given his opinion. My hon. friend, who is also a high authority in his profession, has given another interpretation of the law; but, happily for us, whatever opinion we may entertain, I have reason to believe that the Bill which has been the cause of all this excitement, has met a reverse at one stage of the proceedings.

What may be thrown out at one time by a branch of the United States legislature may pass at another time, so that a temporary relief should hardly be looked upon as a shelving of the whole question, and I can conceive of no stronger argument, on the part of the promoters of the same company, or of a similar company, before a committee or before Congress, than the statement which has been made by the Minister of Justice here. I am not a lawyer, and I do not like to interfere between two lawyers when they disagree; but, even as a matter of law, the Minister of Justice thought that he was absolutely correct. It seems to me that there was nothing to call forth that expression. If it happens not to be correct, and I hope it does not, and it does not seem to be common sense that it should be, we have put a little piece of machinery into the hands of those who are in favour of interfering with the rights of navigation beyond certain limits which we may find it very difficult to meet.

When we were discussing the fact the other night, if 1 understood the gist of the argument, it was contended by some parties that because it was proposed to generate power on a branch of the river that was on the American side, and passing through American territory, neither the International Waterways Commission, nor this House, had any right to interfere. Provided that the level of the water was not raised in the main stream or any branch of it in which navigation was being carried on or

But there were many in this House who held that one branch of the St. Lawrence river was the same as another, and that if we put an obstruction across one branch, it was equivalent to putting an obstruction across the whole stream. I drew attention to this point in the Railway Committee in connection with a Bill giving power to erect a bridge across the Niagara river, which is a navigable stream. It was contended that Canadians did not navigate it, but that Americans did, and that because the plans of the bridge were submitted to the Minister of Public Works, that was sufficient to safeguard the rights of both countries. I contended that it was not, and I contend so still. Since we have an International Waterways Commission, in my opinion, before we pass any legislation affecting those rights, it should be brought to the attention of that commission, so that we may have their views upon it. In this case the approval of the committee was given to the proposed legislation notwithstanding the fact that the Niagara river is a navigable stream. I think that was wrong and out of harmony with the principle discussed here, and I believe generally accepted the other night. If we can get _ any additional information on this subject from the papers to be brought down, it is very desirable that the House should have it, because we cannot too soon have some international understanding as to the extent to which those rights can be interfered with under corporate powers given by this House or by legislative authority in the United States.

To provide for the improvement of navigation in the St. Lawrence river and for the construction of dams, locks, canals, and other appurtenant structures therein at and near Long Sault, Barnhart, and Sheek islands.
Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in Congress assembled, that the Long Sault Development Company, a corporation organized under a law of the state of New Mr. SPROULE.
York, entitled ' An Act to incorporate the Long Sault Development Company, and to authorize said company to construct and maintain dams, canals, power-houses, and locks at or near Long Sault island, for the purpose of improving the navigation of the Saint Lawrence river and developing power from the waters thereof, and to construct and maintain a bridge, and carry on the manufacture of commodities/ which became effective May twenty-third, nineteen hundred and seven, its successors and assigns, be, and they hereby are, authorized to construct, maintain, and operate for navigation, water-power, and other purposes for a period of ninety-nine years a dam or dams in so much of the Saint Lawrence river as lies south of the international boundary line between the United States of America and the Dominion of Canada, near Long Sault, Barnhart, and Sheek islands, either independently or in connection with like works now erected or to be erected in so much of said river as lies north of said international boundary line, with a bridge or bridges and approaches thereto, and a lock or locks, a canal or canals, and other structures appurtenant thereto; provided, that such dam or dams, lock or locks, canal or canals, and other structures appurtenant thereto, except as herein otherwise provided, shall be constructed, maintained, operated, modified, or removed in all respects subject to and in accordance with the provisions of the Act entitled ' An Act to amend an Act entitled " An Act to regulate the construction of dams across navigable waters/ " approved June twenty-third, nineteen hundred and ten: provided further, that such bridge or bridges and approaches thereto, except as herein otherwise provided, shall be constructed, maintained, operated, modified, or removed in all respects subject to and in accordance with the provisions of the Act entitled ' An Act to regulate the construction of bridges over navigable waters/ approved March twenty-third, nineteen hundred and six: and provided further, that the Secretary of War shall cause a survey of that portion of the Saint Lawrence river to be affected by said improvements to be made with a view to securing a navigable channel, suitable for commerce up and down said river, from a point opposite the western end of Croil island to a point opposite the eastern end of Barnhart island, together with plans and specifications therefor, and all rights herein granted to the Long Sault Development Company shall be conditional on its improvement of said channel at its own expense, in accordance with said plans and specifications, said channel to be completed simultaneously with the other works herein authorized, all expenses connected with such survey and the preparation of such plans and specifications to be paid by the said company, its successors, or assigns.
Section 2. That said Long Sault Development Company, its successors and assigns, shall be subject to the provisions of the treaty between the United States and Great Britain relative to the boundary waters between the United States and Canada, proclaimed by the President' of the United States on the thirteenth day of May, nineteen hundred and ten.
Section 3. That the actual construction of the works hereby authorized shall be com-
323"

rnenced within two years and shall be completed within fifteen years from the date of the passage of this Act; otherwise this Act shall be void, and the rights hereby conferred shall cease and be determined.
Section 4. That if said Long Sault Development Company, or any other company or companies acting with it in such development, shall develop power by the construction of works, a part of which shall be located north of the international boundary line, at least one-half of the power generated shall be delivered in the United States. Provided, that when in the opinion of the Secretary of War and the chief of engineers use cannot be found in the United States for the full share thus assigned to this country the surplus may be temporarily diverted to Canada, but shall be returned to the United States when in the opinion of said officers it is needed. Provided further, that nothing herein contained shall be construed to prevent the importation from (Canada of the whole or any part of the power generated from any of the said works in the St. Lawrence river.
Section 5. That should the works hereby authorized be or become at any time, in the opinion of the Secretary of War and the chief of engineers, inadequate to accommodate, or an interference with, the navigation of that portion of the St. Lawrence river affected thereby, said company, its successors or assigns, shall, under the supervision of the Secretary of War and the chief of engineers, make adequate provision for the accommodation of navigation; and should said company, its successors or assigns, fail so to do, the United States government shall, under the supervision of the Secretary of War and the chief of engineers, do anything required to make such provision for navigation, and the expense thereof shall constitute a debt of said company, its successors or assigns, and a lien upon all its property.
Section 6. That the Long Sault Development Company shall execute a bond obligatory on itself, its successors and assigns, with good and solvent sureties in the sum of five hundred thousand dollars, payable to the United States, for the use and benefit of the riparian and other landowners in and along the St. Lawrence river conditioned to pay all damages that may accrue to them, or any of them, by reason of overflow, ice jams and other causes produced by the erection or maintenance of said dam or dams, and the work of construction shall not commence until said bond is executed and approved by the Secretary of War and deposited in the War Department.
Section 7. That the right to alter, amend or repeal this Act is hereby expressly reserv-, ed, and the United States shall incur no liability because of the alteration, amendment or repeal thereof.

speechtext: The Prime Minister will notice that this Bill gives them power to improve the navigation of the St. Lawrence river and to develop power from the waters thereof. It also says they are authorized to construct, maintain and operate for navigation, water-power and other purposes, &c. I mentioned to the Prime Minister last year that the intention of this same company was not only to develop power, that of course is the main thing they have in view, but as I had heard privately from those behind this Bill, to build a canal from the point where they are erecting this dam down to Lake Champlain. This place, Massena, is the last American point on the river, from there down, Canada has both sides of the river, and if they were allowed to let so much water run down and build a canal from Lake Champlain they would make that the foot of navigation for the Americans, bringing grain from Chicago and the west. The minister will remember that discussion, and I do not think any one in the House gave us the impression that there was any truth in that report. The other evening, I happened to be on the train, and, meeting the secretary of the International Waterways Commission, I asked him if any such thing had ever been brought out before their commission. He tola me that it had been, that plans_ and1 all were submitted to this International Waterways Commission, and that our side of the commission had reported against it, and that that report was in the Public Works Department. Should that be the case it is a very serious thing, I think, for our great St. Lawrence route; for, if they get that dam and _ get the canal through such as I mentioned last year, then grain coming from Chicago, Duluth, Port Arthur or any of the upper lake ports can be taken right down to Massena. I asked the secretary how long the canal was. I have forgotten the figures he gave me, but it is not by any means a long canal.

No. But this same company applied for a charter last year, and I believe, at the time, it was pioposed to give them power to dam the St. Lawrence river; but I heard at the time that their whole scheme vr&s to run a canal from where this dam would be, down to Lake Champlain, thus diverting the traffic that now goes to Montreal. If this were true, it would be a very serious thing, and if it were brought to the Prime Minister's attention, the obvious result of such a scheme would surely weigh with Sim to prevent it being carried out. I mention this to-day so that when the matter comes up again, these points may be considered, for these men are sure to come here again and want ;a charter, and, as the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), has said, they are not going to stop with this year's results at Washington. I draw' to the attention of the Prime Minister the statements that have been made to me. I did not ask Mr. Cote to give me any private information; it was a public matter so far as I knew; I was simply discussing this question and asking what the commission had done. I certainly do not wish to reflect upon Mr. Cote.
As to this whole question, we on the St. Lawrence front, feel very strongly. It does not make any difference to me personally, because I am quite a distance from it; but we feel that the great St. Lawrence route should be kept as it is. The steamers stop at Prescott, which is the terminal point from Toronto. Passengers all change there, and it is the very fact of these rapids being there, that brings thousands and thousands of people down that river every year. To give the whole channel into the control of a private corporation, is something about which the people there feel very keenly. In fact, they feel that the Prime Minister will not agree to any such proposition. The damming of the South Sault, which the Prime Minister mentioned the other evening, is also very important. I have talked with engineers of repute on the subject, and they claim that if you raise the river the fifty feet or whatever mav be neces-Mr. REID (Grenville).
sary, it is going to throw the water round into the North Sault, and you cannot tell w'hat the effect may be. Has the Prime Minister ever seen the plan showing the exact location of the islands ? A glance at the map would show that if you dam the South Sault, the water must go by some other way. And we are not going to get any benefit from it. We cannot get the power, for the power is on the American side. The whole St. Lawrence at that particular point is on the American side. Even the North Sault, the rapids down which the Richelieu boats go, is on the American side. If we allow the river to be dammed at that point, we are simply under their control. At the time of the Ashburton Treaty, the parties who framed that treaty certainly went into the matter very carefully and protected our interests at that time. The only reason I can see that has been advanced either to this House or to the country why that charter should be granted is, that power is wanted at Cornwall, Morrisburg, Iroquois, Prescott, Brockville and Kingston. If you go east of the easternmost of these places, you have the Beauharnois canal, and all the powers developed about Lachine. So, I think they have plenty of power there for many years. So far as Cornwall is concerned, I understand that there is no great cry there for more power. I understand that in Cornwall there are some -who would like to see the dam go on for the local benefit that might arise in the way of more manufactures or something of that kind. But I do not think the town is suffering for want of power. As to Morris-burg, they are absolutely against this proposition. Even if there were a power line run in there, they could not use more than a few horse-power. The Hydro-Electric Commission is trying to arrange power for these places. In Prescott, in -which town I live, we are anxious to get power, there is no doubt about that. But to-day you could not sell 500 horse-power in Pres-cctt. While they are very anxious for power, yet they are down on this proposition to dam the St. Lawrence. Speaking from what I have heard, Brockville, -while anxious for power, is not willing to contract for more than 1,500 horse-power with the Hydro-Electric Commission. Kingston, I understand, wants several thousand horse-power. If we have a little patience, I believe that within the next year or two we shall have all the power we want in these places, and much sooner than we could get it by the project of damming the St. Lawrence. They tell me, and I think it is true, that they are developing some power here at Ottawa. The distance from Ottawa to Prescott is 52 miles. From Prescott to where this dam on the St. Lawrence would be built, is at least as far as

that. They are not any nearer to Prescott than we would be from Ottawa. This power will go all over the country. Then there is another power that is being developed; they are getting things in shape, and expect within twelve months, to have from 8,000 to 10,000 horse-power developed north of Kingston. They are trying to make arrangements with the Hydro-Electric Com-missiori to run a line to Kingston, and down to Brockville and Prescott. These powers we have in our own country, they have not been taken up before, and I am quite satisfied that if this matter is held back for two or three years, the towns from Prescott to Kingston will not have any trouble. Kingston is the largest place that wants power, I suppose Kingston might take from 6,000 to 8,000 horse-power. I believe that Kingston is to-day in a position to get that power delivered-the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Harty), will correct me if I am wrong.

There is a company that runs a line from Trenton, they have 100,000 horse-power. Now, I will tell the Prime Minister why I make that statement. A short time ago representatives from Kingston, Gananoque, Brockville and Prescott, and I think the reeves, met a representative of the Hydro-Electric Commission, and the object, I understood, was to find out how much power each municipality would take so he could give them a rate. I saw these gentlemen when they were returning from Toronto; I met one of them with whom I am well acquainted the solicitor for this company, who was there in behalf of this company to oppose the Hydro-Electric scheme; and he told me that his company were prepared to furnish Kingston with all the power they wanted, provided Kingston would give them the absolute franchise, for $25 per horse-power. He gave me the impression that the Kingston people did not want to go into that scheme because they thought the power from the Hydro-Electric would be cheaper. If that is the position of things, it will work out all right in the end for Kingston. Now since these powers are close enough to be developed, and to be brought into these places, and will be brought in within the next year or two, I think we in this House need not pass 'any legislation of this kind. It may be that in twenty years from now the position of this country will be changed. But unless there is some strong reason why that Bill should be passed in this House other than those I have mentioned, I think this government and every member of this House should strongly oppose it, and leave our rights to that river just as they are at the present time. Therefore, I hope the Prime Minister will do everything he can to leave us exactly
in the same position we are. Perhaps he has already done it, I do not want to ask him to reveal any state secret, but I hope he has wired Ambassador Bryce to ask the President not to allow that Bill to go through at all, but that the rights we have under the Ashburton Treaty may be preserved to us intact. I am satisfied if the Premier does that, the Bill will never go through the American Congress, and I do not think these people would trouble this House again at any future time. The men who are promoting this scheme are very persistent. They were in my county, and they didn't hesitate to say that they had a million dollars, or two million dollars if necessary, with which to put this Bill through. They were up along the whole country, talking to the people, trying to raise an agitation, and to force the members from that region to put this Bill through. I think the means they took were as unfair as were ever resorted to by the promoters of any Bill.

speechtext: I am glad of the opportunity of saying a few words for the purpose of affirming the position I took when this question was discussed the other night in the House. I was then opposed both by the Minister of Public Works and by the head of the government. I was proceeding with an argument when I was interrupted, and was told that this power on the Long Sault had already been conveyed to a corporation. I began to argue that under the Ashburton Treaty the Crown had not the power of conveying that property without the consent of the legislature, and I was told by the Minister of Public Works and by the Prime Minister that the legislature had already consented to a conveyance. I was astounded at the time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: IN THE SENATE OP THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: I did not say that.

subtopic: IN THE SENATE OP THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
The Minister of Public Works said it, and I thought the right hon. gentleman assented. I took the opportunity of looking up the case, and I found that no such power had been given to any company in the world for the use of the Long Sault canal. My position then was perfectly right. Under the Ashburton Treaty, navigation and what is essential to navigation, is reserved to the people of this country, and the Crown cannot convey it. What the Crown did convey in reference to that work near Sheik island, is the right of user to the surplus water, the discharge of the by-wash that is used for the purpose of keeping tihe level of Sheik island. There is a certain by-wash passing down there, a surplus of water. That water, so far as it did not interfere with navigation, was leased to an individual or to a corporation. The Act of parliament was simply an en-powering one, giving to the corporation the

right of doing what the individual, or the party to whom that property was conveyed, had the right of doing.
There is that further right because the parties who leased that particular property from the Crown had in mind the contingency that perhaps they might not have water enough. The original idea of building the canal there was to utilize what is called Hoople's creek. The idea was to deepen and dredge Hoople's creek so as to utilize it for the purposes of navigation instead of building an outside embankment. Under the contract with this corporation the government have given them the right to deepen that creek to any extent they like and the use of whatever water may be diverted from the St. Lawrence. That power is given to this corporation but it does not interfere at all with any of the rights which we have under the Ashburton Treaty. Every one knows that the particular part of the St. Lawrence between Sheik island and the north shore was utilized for the operation of a little mill owned by Mr. Snetsinger. That mill was expropriated when the canal was being built and taken over by the government. It was to a certain extent utilizing that power, or the power which has been developed by the erection of a dam. The ownership of that power rests with the people of Canada and the people of the United States, and it cannot be taken either by Crown - gift, or in any other way, unless with the consent of the legislature of this country. It is true that under the treaty we have given to the In ternational Commission the right of deciding what shall be done with these particular waterways, how they shall be utilized, and to what extent we have a right in them. My hon. friend who spoke before me referred to those powers as being situated in the United States, and he said that if the water was dammed the power would be of great benefit to the United States for the simple reason that the body was situated on the United States side. That question arose in connection with the power question at Niagara Falls. It came before the Waterways Commission, and I think they arrived at a perfectly proper -and right conclusion when they determined that no matter whether international waterways diverged in their course to the south or the north, or whether the large body of water was situated on one side or the -other a moiety of the power should belong to each country, and that each would have a common interest in it. So that, if any dam be erected on the south side for the purpose of utilizing that power, a moiety, or half, would belong to each country, and they would not be allowed to utilize it by the Waterways Commission in the first instance unless they had received the assent of this parliament and of the Congress of Mr. HAGGART (Lanark).
th(e United States. So, I think it is perfectly secure. The possibilities of the future are very vague and uncertain as to its ever being utilized as a power. The United States Senate has thrown out the Bill but it is quite true that it may -be introduced again. No power can be given to that company unless with the consent of this legislature and especially unless with the consent of the government and the consent of the Waterways Commission. I think the day is far distant when such a consent could be shown to be advisable. If we want power in this country, as my hon. friend says, there are hundreds of other places which can be utilized, the development of which will not interfere with the scenic grandeur such as that which characterizes the St. Lawrence. There are other places where power can be as cheaply developed and -at the same time without spoiling the natural beauty of the place. This is an heirloom that ought to be kept for the people of this country. With reference to navigation, this is one of the wonders of the trip down the St. Lawrence that annually attracts more passengers than anything else, and unless the gravest and most serious reasons are shown from an economic point of view that it is in the interests of the country that this dam should be erected, I think the unanimous opinion of the country from one end to the other will be that we should leave this place in its present state of nature.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I happen to represent the constituency in which it is proposed to construct these works. I have observed that in the discussions which have taken place in this House, and other places a very great deal of misapprehension often occurs as to the actual situation, and as to what is actually proposed to be done. In the first place, if I caught correctly the purport of the Bill which has -been introduced at Washington and which has been read by the hon. member for Grenville (Mr. Reid), the proposition there is to dam the whole St. Lawrence. If that is the proposition I do not think that my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Sir Allen Aylesworth) would argue for a moment that that could be done at the instance of the United States authorities without consulting the parliament of Canada. As I understood the remarks of the Minister of Justice the other evening, he contended that it would not be impossible for the American government to give the necessary authority for the damming of the South Sault alone without consulting the government of this country. Now, in giving that opinion I observed that the Minister of Justice compared the South Sault with the channel of the river that had already been dammed by this government in the construction of the

Cornwall canal, and lie apparently drew the inference that 'because that had been done without consulting the American government the same rule should apply to damming the -South Sault under the authority of the American government. I do not know how familiar the Minister of Justice may be with the facts as they exist at that ipoint, but I certainly know that there is no comparison at all between the two streams. The channel of the river which was dammed by the Canadian government is an entirely different stream from the channel of the South Sault. The South Sault is a channel that has always been navigated by steamers on the down trip. It is navigated to-day by ships of our own country as well as by ships of the United States ; in fact, I think, although I will not be positive in the statement, that any host that navigates the big Sault on the Canadian side can navigate the small Sault on the American side of the river. So, the situation is entirely different with regard to the channel of the river that was dammed for the purpose of the Cornwall canal. That is a channel that has never been navigated by any class of vessels except by the flat bottomed scows which in early days, before any canal was built there at all, were towed along the banks of the river by horses. No steamer ever ran up or down that channel that has -been dammed by the Canadian government. I think that possibly that circumstance was not called to the attention of the Minister of Justice, and that if it had been he might have drawn a distinction between the damming of one channel and the damming of the other. There was a great deal of alarm on the American side of the river at the time the Canadian government proposed to dam that channel. I cannot remember that there was any official opposition, but I do know that there was a very strong agitation on the American side of the river, that the American government was appealed to, and I understand that in some way or other the American government took the necessary steps to investigate and satisfy themselves that no possible damage to navigation could occur from the blocking of the Canadian channel that was dammed for the purpose of the Cornwall canal. *

speechtext: At what point did this blocking occur that the hon. gentleman speaks of?

subtopic: IN THE SENATE OP THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: I refer to the Sheik island dams which block one of the channels of the river on the Canadian side. That is a very small stream. It was navigated at one time by those flat-bottomed scows that were towed by horses but steamers never navigated that channel.

subtopic: IN THE SENATE OP THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: At what time did this agitation take place? Is it of recent date?

subtopic: IN THE SENATE OP THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: The agitation took place at the time it was proposed to construct the Sheik island dams. I do not know that it ever went to the extent of an official inquirv on behalf of the American government, to the authorities here, but the hon. gentleman from Lanark (Mr. Hag-gart) would know that, because, when-the dam was commenced, I think he was Minister of Railways and Canals. The hon. member for South Lanark has stated that the Act incorporating the St. Lawrence Power Company did not give authority to create any of these dams, and in that opinion I entirely concur. I do not think there ever was such a dam in contemplation then, and I do not think the wording of the Act in any way authorizes the damming of the St. Lawrence at that point. What was in contemplation was a different scheme altogether, and the dams that were referred to were the wing dams which were to be thrown out into the stream for the purpose of diverting the water. What I think is very clear is that there is no authority from the Canadian parliament whatever to create those dams that have for their object the complete damming of the St. Lawrence river. As I understand the Ashburton Treaty, we have the same rights of navigation on all these water s as the Americans themselves have, regardless of whether the channel happens to be in American or Canadian waters. A great many people talk of these channels being entirely in American waters, but as a matter of fact every vessel that navigates the Big Sault has first to go through entirely Canadian waters, and after it goes through the rapids it crosses into American waters. There is no such thing as navigating the Big Sault without being at one time in Canadian territory and at another time in American territory. In the Big Sault channel of the rapids themselves is entirely in Canadian territory.

subtopic: IN THE SENATE OP THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman means that they are on the Canadian side or the open channel between Long Sault island and the Canadian shore?

subtopic: IN THE SENATE OP THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: Yes. The channel at that point on the Big Sault i3 entirely in Canadian waters, and, of course, the South Sault is entirely in American waters from start to finish.

subtopic: IN THE SENATE OP THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: There are no American waters, or - Canadian waters, under the Ashburton Treaty ; both countries have an equal right to navigate.

subtopic: IN THE SENATE OP THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: I am referring to the boundary line

speechtext:
The hon. gentleman understands the situation, and I would ask him if it is not a fact that on account of the winding of the river there is a point

m the rapids where the whole of the channel is wholly in American territory?
Mr. SMITH (Stormont)'. Yes. After you pass through the rapids proper you cross at the head of Barnhart island, which is an American island, and from there down the channel is between Barnhart island and the American shore, entirely in American territory. There is a small channel called the Little River, which is not navigable even for canoes, and which goes between Barnhart island and the Canadian island called Sheik island. I think, therefore, it is quite clear that before any complete damming of the St. Lawrence river can be accomplished there must be authority given by the government of this country. The question has been raised as to whether that authority oan be given iby the Governor in Council without submitting it to parliament, or whether parliament has to be consulted, and that is a question I shall not deal with on this occasion. The Minister of Justice, as I understood him the other evening, confined his remarks to the damming of the South Sault alone. If what he set out on that occasion is good constitutional law, namely, that the Americans can-do that without consulting us at all, then it is rather an unfortunate positipn for us. If they can dam it without consulting us at all they probably will not be under the necessity of dividing the power with us. I hope the Minister of Justice is not right in that respect, because it is possible to develop very considerable power by the damming of the South Sault alone, and if we have the right in common with the Americans to the navigation of these waters we probably would have the right to say they could only dam them upon the terms of giving us one-half of the power. Representing as I do the constituency in which this development is supposed to take place, I am exceedingly anxious to know that if there is any development of any kind on either channel we should have one-half of that power available in my part of the country. I am in hopes that in view of the difference between that channel and the channel that was dammed by the Canadian government, to which I have alluded, the Minister of Justice will be able to form a different opinion from that which he expressed in the House the other evening. Now, it has been represented by the engineers that some 500,000 horse-power can be developed at that point by the damming of the whole channel, and they tell us that about 60,000 of that 500,000 can be developed in the South Sault and the remainder in the Big, or North Sault. I am not here to-day to say that I desire the Bill before the authorities at Washington to go through, or that I desire any scheme to go through, because, first and foremost, I want to know the terms. If, without injuring navigation, we Mr. REID (Grenville).
could develop 400,000, or 500,000 horsepower in the St. Lawrence river at that point and could secure one-half of that for Canada, and could secure at the same time the absolute control of that power for all time, so that Canadian consumers could have it upon proper terms, then I say I am in favour of any scheme of that kind. But I am not in favour of any scheme that will hand over to an American corporation all this power; to do what they like with it, to take it to the American side, or to control and monopolize it for all time. A scheme of that kind I would think it my duty to condemn. But if power can be developed upon the terms of securing one-half of it for the Canadian people for all time, so that there can be no monopoly, then I am in favour of such development. If 60,000 horse-power can be developed in the South Sault it follows that 440,000 horse-power can be developed on the North Sault. If we leave the South Sault out, and if there is development on the Big Sault, the South Sault will supply all the needs of navigation, just as they have it to-day; it will accommodate every vessel that navigates the Big Sault, and will leave an open channel to prevent all this flooding that some people are so much afraid of. In that way they could develop 440,000 horse-power without interrupting navigation at all, or closing the natural channel of the St. Lawrence.

subtopic: IN THE SENATE OP THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman's remarks are very interesting and very instructive. Would ha specify from what point to what point the dam would be built?

subtopic: IN THE SENATE OP THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
Just where the promoters suggest: across the Large Sault from the foot of Long Sault island to the head of Barnhart's. That would dam the Big Sault. Then if you dam from the foot of Barnhart's to the Canadian shore you have a dam across the whole northern channel, and you leave the southern channel, that is the South Sault, entirely open for navigation without obstructing the Richelieu boats, or any boats that would navigate that river. Then you would have an open channel which would absolutely prevent any such flooding as has been feared bv the people of Morrisburg and by the people in the county of Grenville. Now, that is a scheme which I would like to see carried out, provided it could be carried out on the terms I mention, that is<, that absolute security would be given that one-half of the power would be available for all time in Canada, with proper authority given to this government to enforce that, and proper regulation of the rates by our Railway Commission or some other competent authority. We would then have the opportunity of controlling for all time one-half of the water-power in case the pro-

moters refused to carry out that part of the bargain. In fact, I think the only permanent security we can have that one-half of the water-power developed would be available for Canadians would be that we would have the opportunity, without calling upon the owners, of tapping that channel ourselves and creating one-half of the water-power. If that power were vested in the government, there would be an absolute security that our right to one-half of the power would be conserved.

speechtext: Suppose the power were developed, where is the present demand for power, and is it not a fact that there is a lot of power in the St. Lawrence within 30 or 40 miles of Cornwall?

speechtext: I will answer my hon. friend by citing the case of Messina, which, before the creation of its waterpower, was not any larger than the town my hon. friend represents, Prescott. There was not a single industry there. Some English capitalists started to construct a power canal right opposite Massena, and everybody wanted to know what they intended to do, as nobody within many miles of Massena wanted power. The company went on and built the canal, and today the very agitation which we hear so much about is due to the fact that 60,000 horse-power is not half eB.ough for the village of Massena.

subtopic: IN THE SENATE OP THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: Then the hon. gentleman is asking for this power in order that it will build up Cornwall?

subtopic: IN THE SENATE OP THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: I do not know whether it would build up Cornwall any more that it would build up Prescott, because all that would be necessary to carry the power to Prescott would be to run two wires along the shore.

subtopic: IN THE SENATE OP THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: The power would be cheaper at Cornwall?

subtopic: IN THE SENATE OP THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: There would be just the difference between transmitting it five or six miles to Cornwall and about 50 miles to Prescott. In fact, there would be power enough developed to supply every town in eastern Ontario, and at a price that no power which my hon. friend has in mind could compare with at all. The development of the whole of eastern Ontario depends on how cheaply the power could be had.

subtopic: IN THE SENATE OP THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman in a position to state what the effect would be on the river above the Long Sault island? How far up would the dam affect the stream, and what would be the effect of it in the flooding season in the spring?

subtopic: IN THE SENATE OP THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
As a matter of fact, we do not have a flood season in the spring along the St. Lawrence river. That
is one of its peculiarities. The difference in the height of Lake Ontario and Lake St. Francis varies only three or four feet from one season to another. The only season of flood on the St. Lawrence is in the middle of the winter, caused by the ice jamming for a time in the narrow channel of the river, and thus causing the water above it to rise.

subtopic: IN THE SENATE OP THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: It occurs when the ice is breaking up.

subtopic: IN THE SENATE OP THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: Not when the ice is breaking up. The ice jams occur usually in the month of February. The hon. gentleman asked me how high we proposed to raise the water. The stipulation that was made by the Department of Railways and Canals was that under no circumstances should the water be raised high enough to interfere with the Cornwall canal, which is supplied above the rapids. The hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton last year discussed the possibility of the water of the St. Lawrence rising so high as to cross to the Ottawa river.

subtopic: IN THE SENATE OP THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: No, flowing into the Raisin above Lancaster.

subtopic: IN THE SENATE OP THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
Speaking candidly, I am indebted to my hon. friend for puting me right on these matters, with which I do Mr. LENNOX.
not profess to be familiar. It is not mere empty compliment for me to say that both by reason of his familiarity with the territory, and by reason of his facility of expression, the hon. gentleman has certainly added very much to the store of knowledge that we have upon this very important question. Now, the circumstance I have just pointed out is an additional reason why I propose to object to the line of argument taken by the Minister of Justice the other day, and in saying that we are-aside from conventions of recent date-practically at the mercy of the United States as to what should be done with the St. Lawrence river.
I listened with attention to the hon. gentleman who has just spoken, and who has evidently given this matter a good deal of consideration. His opinion is that it would probably be in the interest of both Canada and the United States that the scheme proposed at the present time should be carried out, but with this qualification, that he would leave open the channel which lies immediately alongside the American shore. He thinks it would be in the interest of Canada and of the United States to dam the St. Lawrence river from the Long Sault island across to Barnhart island, and then across to the Canadian shore. True, the hon. gentleman qualified his opinion by, saying that such a scheme should be subject always to the paramount consideration of navigation; in other words, that provided we can still effectually navigate the river, both Canada and the United States would be benefited by the development of the enormous amount of power, some 460,000 horse-power, to be equally divided between the two countries. With that part of his argument I cannot agree. I am entirely opposed to damming the St. Lawrence river by any private or corporate scheme. I believe that, having regard to the great gift of providence in the possession of the St. Lawrence river, in view of the increasing interest and benefit it will be to the people of Canada as a navigable water, having regard to the fact which is being emphasized all the time that water navigation is beyond all comparison cheaper for bulky commodities than is transportation by rail, we never should consent, to the damming of that great river. Although we have for the moment escaped the assaults of this enormous company which stands behind the Long Sault Development Company, with its capital of $50,000,000, buttressed, fortified and encouraged by certain patriotic gentlemen on the Canadian side, endorsed as it is by the Minister of Public Works-although we have for the moment escaped from these people, it is unfortunate indeed that the Minister of Justice threw out the remarks he did the other night, telling the people

of the United States for all time to come, by the voice of the Canadian Minister of Justice, that we are practically without remedy as regards the broadest and most important feature of this international question. The Minister of Justice started out by telling us that this was a matter of international law. That is all right. But he followed that by asking:	What is international law? And he replied that international law was an indeterminate thing something that it is almost impossible to find out; ill other words, that no one can say what international law is. Well, Sir, that is a new doctrine. It is true, as the Minister of Justice said, that international law is not contained in any statute, and it is equally true that many questions of international law may arise upon which there has been no decision, matters of new import may arise in reference to boundary waters which have to be construed and determined by analogy and upon principle. But to tell us in effect, as he did, that we are practically at sea as regards anything to guide us in this matter, I venture to say will be found upon investigation not to be correct. I venture to suggest to the Minister of Justice, that since many rivers are international boundaries in Europe and other countries, the question of what are the rights of the parties on each side of the river, is not a new question by any means, although it is new in this particular phase. ^A large and important volume of international law, and of views and decisions on similar questions, have been recognized by nations and will be found applicable to the question here under discussion. Be that as it may, whether the law laid down by the Minister of Justice is correct or not, I regret, speaking from a national point of view, that the Minister of Justice has declared to the people of the United States, as a rule which they will invoke in future, that we are practically at their mercy in reference to this matter. He says that aside from convention we are practically helpless, that the only remedy for us is expostulation, that as suppliants only can we endeavour to prevent _ whatever the United States may determine to do in reference to this matter. Well, I do not think so. If I say it outspokenly, I say it all the same with due deference to the great legal learning of my hon. friend the Minister of Justice. But I venture still to say that we are not in the hands of the United States in that regard. The law of nations is as strong in support of justice now as it ever was. It has been many years since when a small community could not rely upon securing their rights at the hands of a larger community, if they could show that their cause was just.
Now the Minister of Justice proceeded to point out, by inference if not in words, that by reason of the fact that we had 103J
dammed the channel upon the north side of Sheik island, we w^ere powerless, even as a matter of justice and fair-play, to1 protest against the damming of the waters south of the international boundary. I deny that proposition altogether. Why, what the Minister of Justice subsequently read put that question at rest. It showed that by the recent treaty, provision was made as to the future, that, although all cases that had already occurred were closed, as to the future neither party could interfere with the height of the water upon either side, recognizing by the treaty to which the Minister of Justice referred, that we were conceded, if we did not originally have it, the right to have matters remain in statu quo, and that, as far as our damming of that little trickling stream at Sheik island was concerned, it had nc bearing at all upon the question of the damming of those navigable channels which the development company seeks power to dam at this time. The Minister! of Justice, in an elaborate and very carefully worded argument, referred to Article III. of the new Waterways Treaty, for the purpose of emphasizing and fortifying his position that we are absolutely at the mercy of the United States, except in so far as the matter can be regulated by section 3 of the Waterways Commission and that section 3 only applied to the question of the height of the water. The Minister of Justice sent forth to the United States- and it will be of record there for all time to come in their archives and will be invoked, as I would remind the right hon. gentleman who leads the House, against us either in reference to this river or other-rivers when we come to anpeal to the provisions of the Ashburton Treaty-the solemn declaration that we have practically no control over this great international waterway except such as is provided for by section 3 of the Waterways Treaty-a statement, as an hon. gentleman reminds me, that it is in the interests of the United States people, and not only that, Sir, but a statement that it was absolutely unnecessary to make, and which has almost the force and effect of a statute when you come to negociate with a foreign nation upon a matter of this kind in the future, By the _ sturdy opposition put up by His Majesty's loyal opposition we succeeded, first, in repelling the efforts of the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) last year in support of this measure, which was absolutely against the interests of the people of Canada, and although we may have, by our timely note of warning the other day, done something to prevent this measure from being passed by the United States Senate, yet the evil remains, and in all future discussions between Canada and the United States in

settling these boundary waterway questions, we, on this side of the House, when we are on the right of the Speaker, as well, as hon. gentlemen who are now carrying on the affairs of the country, will be con-, fronted by the utterance of the Minister of Justice made upon that occasion. _ Let me read just a line from what the Minister of Justice said:
The provision of article three of the new Waterways Treaty is to the effect that in addition to existing obstructions, no further obstructions, whether temporary or permanent, of boundary waters on either side of the line -and the whole river is a boundary water from main shore to main shore-no new obstruction on either side affecting the natural level or flow of the boundary waters on the other side of the line shall be made except by the authority of the United States or the Dominion of Canada, within their respective jurisdictions and with the approval of the International Joint Commission.
I wish to point out here that the wording of this section is that no new obstruction shall be made. The minister proceeds to say:
Now the wording of that exception plainly implies that each country, within its own jurisdiction, has the right to authorize obstructions in waters such as these.
That is the conclusion that the Minister of Justice laid down the other day, that is the statement that he sent forth to the United States. He says:
Now, the wording of that exception plainly implies that each country, within its own jurisdiction has the right to authorize obstructions in waters such as these. No new obstructions, it says, shall be made affecting the natural level on the other side of the line except by the authority of the United States or the Dominion within their respective jurisdictions.
So the argument of the Minister of Justice, as you will remember, Mr. Speaker, and as it has gone on record, was that we; are practically at the mercy of the United States except as to whatever relief we can get out of the third section of the treaty referred to, and that section is confined solely and exclusively to the question of the height of the water. That, J venture to say wdth great deference, is not the law. I pointed out then to the Minister of Jus-i tice the provisions of section 7 of the Ashburton Treaty, and it is only fair to say that upon that being called to his attention, the minister, in a very faint way, it is true, suggested there might be some possible relief there. The hon. gentleman asked me to read the provision of the Ashburton Treaty, and I read it now as I read it the other day.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: IN THE SENATE OP THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
I think there is no practical utility in discussing at the present time the general merits or demerits of damming the St. Lawrence river at the Long Sault. There is no proposition, at any rate at present, before us, or any tribunal so far as I am aware of for the building of a dam in Canadian waters, or upon the Canadian side of the boundary. The only room at present which existed at all for discussing this scheme was in reference to the proposal to dam the south channel at a place which was solely within United States territory. If the morning newspapers are correct, that proposition has been defeated in the United States House of Representatives, and is at an end for the present at all events. But with regard to that proposal, in the discussion which took place in this House on Thursday last, I expressed the opinion which I entertained as to the legal rights of Canada to interfere, or to take exception to what was proposed. I vfas speaking altogether, of course speaking altogether, of the proposal to build a dam wholly upon United States soil and upon that side of the boundary, and speaking of that proposal without any reference to the continuation of that dam by the building of additional or subsidiary structures at some future time upon Canadian soil, I was looking at the matter as though it were an independent proposition to dam this southernmost chan-

nel of the St. Lawrence upon United States territory alone. Looking at it from that point of view from the standpoint of international rights, the position which I took was that in the absence of a treaty-supposing there was no treaty affecting the matter at all- there would be no ground upon which we could in any way interfere. Bat that is a purely academic situation. There are treaties, and, therefore, it was of interest to consider what our situation would have been had there been no treaties only with a view to showing what the foundation might be of any rights which we possessed. Taking the treaties as they stand-both the Ashburton Treaty and the treaty of last year with regard to international waterways- they make our rights in this matter, it seems to me, reasonably clear. I was somewhat astonished in looking over the ' Hansard ' report of the debate which took place on this subject last Thursday to see the impression which my hon. friend from St. Anne (Mr. Doherty) had derived from what I said, and I am afraid from what I have been able to gather of what has been said to-day, that my good friend from Stormont (Mr. Smith) has not comprehended as I would have wished him to have comprehended what I then said. I certainly meant to make it as distinct as words could be that the rights of navigation were supreme, and that if this proposal interfered with navigation there was an end of the matter. We then have undoubted right to object, and in everything which I said on Thursday last I was basing my remarks upon the supposition that the promoters were able to do what they wished to do without affecting navigation in any injurious way. I think I was clear upon that. At column 2969 of ' Hansard,' after discussing the question whether or not the level on the Canadian side would necessarily be raised by this work, and after stating that assuming the level on the Canadian side was not raised when the interests of navigation are the only things to be considered,
I said:
That is exactly the situation under the existing treaties. The right of navigation is paramount and that right is secured. That right exists in this United States channel which it is proposed to dam, just as it exists in the old channel between Sheik's island and the mainland of Ontario which is to-day utilized as part of our Cornwall canal. The right of navigation is secured by treaty and is not proposed to be interfered with. On the contrary, it is proposed to be helped according to the plans of the promoters, and unless the right of navigation is interfered with, or the level altered on our own side, we have, under existing treaties, no cause to object.
Now, with regard to the paramount right of navigation, the language of the Ashburton Treaty as given to the House in the debate to which I refer by the hon. gentleman from North
Simcoe, secures to us an equal right with the right of the United States. Some gentlemen who participated in the debate last week seemed to entertain the view that the terms of the Ashburton Treaty precluded the placing of any obstruction in navigable waters, and secured forever the free and open navigation of the whole of the waters of the St. Lawrence from main shore to main shore. I do not think that is the language of the treaty. The language is, speaking compendiously, that the channel from main shore to main shore shall be equally free and open to the ships, vessels and boats of both parties. It might be paraphrased in this way: shall be as free and open to the ships, vessels and boats of one party as to those of the other party. So long as the equal right to the navigation of the channels on either side is afforded by the country in which those channels are, to the boats, vessels and ships of the other country, I see no infraction of the terms of the Ashburton Treaty. We did not consider, when we shut of the channel between Sheik's island and the county of Stormont, that we were encroaching upon the prohibition of the Ashburton Treaty. We turned that channel into a canal. We left it, as we found it, as free and open to the navigation of the United States vessels as it was to the navigation of Canadian vessels. It might have been argued that we were obstructing the navigation. True, we did build an embankment across the entrance to it, and in that sense we prevented any one coming from the main channel of the Long Sault with his boat into the Canadian channel to the north of Sheik's island.

subtopic: IN THE SENATE OP THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: Had we not a canal to the north of Sheik's island before the Ashburton Treaty?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: IN THE SENATE OP THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: Our canal was on the mainland to the north of the channel which in a state of nature lay between Sheik's island and the mainland. Our canal opposite Sheik's island was. cut out of the mainland.

subtopic: IN THE SENATE OP THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: Had we not a canal before the Ashburton Treaty?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: IN THE SENATE OP THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: I think very likely. What I am pointing out is that long after the Ashburton Treaty we, for our own purposes, obstructed the upper entrance into the natural channel which lay between Sheik's island and the mainland, and, by a dam which we built from Sheik's island to the mainland, prevented any vessel coming into that natural channel from the main stream.

subtopic: IN THE SENATE OP THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: Was that act in contravention of any treaty between Canada and the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think not.
I think we had a perfect right to do it, because after it was done we left the navigation of that channel as free and open to the United States as it was to us; and, on exactly the same principle, so long as the United States leaves its southernmost channel as free and open to us as it is to them,
I cannot see how the terms of the Ashburton Treaty are interfered with. We have, however, not only the Ashburton Treaty, but we have the recent Waterways Convention, under which this very stream, from main shore to main shore, is to be forever free and open and common to the ships of both nations for the purposes of navigation. Navigation is made the paramount consideration under the Waterways Treaty. The new International Commission is told by that agreement between the two nations that its first consideration, apart from the use of water for domestic or sanitary purposes, is to be the use of it for purposes of navigation. The use of it for purposes of manufacturing power is an after consideration altogether. Now, by that recent treaty we have additional rights. We have not only our former right in regard to navigation maintained and confirmed, but we have the additional engagement on the part of the United States that although their government or Congress may authorize such an obstruction as that which is proposed, that obstruction cannot be allowed to be built in the river if the effect of it will ibe to alter the level on our side, unless the assent of the International Commission is first obtained. That is an additional protection and safeguard, and, in what I said on Thursday last, I was not for a moment losing sight of the paramount interests of navigation. On the contrary, I thought I was putting them in the forefront in saying what I did, speaking throughout on the assumption that the interests of navigation would not be in the least degree impaired by this proposed work. With regard to the sharing between the two countries of power, if power is to be created at this place, this is not a matter which is dealt with by any existing convention between the two nations as far as I am aware. It is a matter for subsequent negotiations and if possible agreement; and if it ever becomes a question of building a dam on Canadian territory to supplement or improve the dam which has been suggested to be built on United States territory, there will certainly be the very best opportunity on our part to make terms and conditions. But until there is a practical proposition of that character before this House for consideration, it seems to me that the discussion of the matter is entirely of an academic or theoretical nature.

Minister of Justice intended to convey in his observations of the other day, when I understood him to lay down the absolute proposition that we were not entitled to complain of the obstruction of these channels, though he did make a proviso to the effect that that was so, srt long as the navigation was not interfered with; and I think that I acknowledged that.
