Minister of Justice laid down the proposition that, in the existing circumstances of this matter pending before the American Congress, where authority was sought on the part of a private company to dam the channels on both sides of the Long Sauls island, we have no ground, whatever, L, intervene or even to expostulate. I understand the hon. Minister of Justice to-day to contend that in his observations of the other day he did not go so far as to say that if there was danger that there was a question of obstruction of navigation, we had absolutely no ground to stand on. He says at page 2971:
In the circumstances which exist, Mr. Speaker, I think it would be difficult fqr us to frame any line of diplomatic objection or remonstrance which would have any effective foundation. It conld at once be answered by the United States that, under the terms or our treaty, we have the right to consider the advisability of doing this, and yon are perfectly protected by the creative of tins International Joint Commission upon which you are equally represented.
So'I think we were at least excusable foi understanding that the Minister of J us-tice, with all the circumstances just as they stand before him, had committed himself to the proposition that we had absolutely no ground upon which we could stand to intervene to claim protection for any right of ours in connection with the proposed barring of these two channels. That seemed to me at the time, and I must confess it still seems to me, a rather extraordinary position 'to take on the part of the government that is charged with the protection of the interests of this country. Here was a proposition to bar or dam these channels. It is quite true, if I understood properly the reading of the Bill today, that the company that asked for this right to dam these channels, did say that they were going to make some other provision whereby, notwithstanding their damming the channel, a means would be afforded for navigating one of those channels; but surely Canada was interested, and is interested in that measure or would be still interested if that measure were still being proposed, and I think it is not going too far to say. we should be consulted as to whether this method which this company was saying it was going to pro-

vide in lieu of leaving us facilities for navigation, such as they would have been if the channels were left free and open, was, or was not sufficient to effect the purpose. That was a matter of very vital importance to Canada. I do not think it is necessary to go so far as to interpret the terms of the Ashburton Treaty as meaning that these two channels must remain absolutely in the condition in which they were at the time the treaty was made. I quite recognize that there .might be some interference with those channels which would not affect their availability for purposes of navigation, and I would not be interested to contend on behalf of Canada that, assuming that what was going to be done, was going to leave those channels available for navigation, we would need to resist what was going to be done. But that is one thing, and it is another thing to say that when it is proposed to dam these channels, to take away from us the right given us under the terms of the treaty (and that is justified by the suggestion that something else is going* to be provided, that would be just as good) that we have no interest in that proposition, that we have no locus standi before the body that was called upon to give those powers, that we have no right and no interest to be heard before that body before it decides upon the essential question of whether this damming of the channels, which prima facie, is an interference with navigation, is, or is not, in view of the particular remedies which this company says it .proposes to give, going to produce an interference with navigation and an interference with our rights. While I still fail to see in the statement of the Minister of Justice to-day any withdrawal of that utterance, I do not think that our right to bo heard upon this matter, to look into this matter, to point out, if we so ascertained that the proposition did involve an interference with navigation, is at all diminished or affected by what the Minister has just said. It might be that, upon our being heard, we might satisfy ourselves that there was no interference with navigation. That might happen, but assuredly, it was a matter in which we had a vital interest and in which I would think the government would have felt it incumbent upon them to see that those interests were protected and that we were heard before this matter was disposed of in the manner proposed.
In so far as the Minister of Justice bases the proposition that we have nothing to say with regard to obstructions to be made ir these two southern channels on the ground that they are entirely upon American territory, and upon the fact that we constructed a canal which obstructed the channel between Sheik island and the
mainland, it seems to be only necessary to point out that the provision of the Ashburton Treaty said absolutely nothing about the channel between Sheik island and the mainland to make it quite clear that what we did to that channel can afford no ground for arguing a similar right on the part of the United States to do the same thing in the other channels. Because it is a remarkable fact (presumably attributable to the reason suggested by the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Haggart) that the Cornwall canal existed before the Ashburton Treaty), that the Ashburton Treaty makes no reference whatever to that channel between Sheik island and the mainland. It is not a treaty for the purpose of establishing equal rights for both parties in the waters of both parties; it is a specific provision to secure to Canada equal rights of navigation with the United States in channels which are in the United States. It is not at all a mere reciprocal arrangement that the river shall be, from side to side, equally free to the navigation of both parties, it is a provision for Canada that the .specified channels in the St. Lawrence on both sides of the Long Sault island and of Barnhart island shall be equally free and open to navigation. So that what we did on the channel between Sheik island and the mainland could have no possible bearing on what the United States had the right to do on the two channels with regard to which they had bound themselves that they should remain equally free and open to navigation to the vessels of our country and of theirs. There is absolutely no parity in the situation. It might be iso if we were governed solely by the recent Boundary Waters Commission Treaty.
As regards the argument that the words ' equally free and open,' do not give us a right to have these channels remain absolutely open just as they were, as I said a moment ago, I do not think it is necessary for the purpose of supporting the rights of Canada to go so far as to contend that the words mean that the two channels are to remain just as they were with no obstruction in any portion of them. On the other hand, do I understand the Minister of Justice seriously to contend that provided these channels are equally closed to both countries, this treaty has not been violated? Has the United States, which has agreed with us that these channels should be equally open to the navigation of the vessels belonging to citizens of both countries, a right to say to us: Well, if we do dam the channels they are just as open to you as to us. But they are not open to anybody at all. I hardly think that such an interpretation -would be seriously contended for. I quite understand that it may be consistent with what is stipulated there that some modification, or

obstruction if you will, in some portion of these channels might exist, and that we would be without ground of complaint, provided always that they remained open to navigation, and just as open to us as to the citizens of the United States. I must confess, though we have sometimes heard some criticism of the contentions which our American friends make upon diplomatic questions, I do not believe, so far as my knowledge goes, that they have ever resorted to what would seem to me to be such a manifest quibble as that, and I would be sorry to attribute to them the capability of seeking to encroach upon our clear rights by resorting to such an argument as that.
To sum it all up, this seems, to me to be the clear situation. We are precisely with regard to the United States, and with regard to these channels, in the position of a man whose neighbour has undertaken with him that two roads running over the neighbour's property should be for all time as free and open to the party in whose favour the obligation was contracted as to the party who owned the land; and in that situation the neighbour who has consented to these roads running over his own land, proceeds to build barricades across them, and he couples that action with the statement: Well, I am making a gate there, and I will pass you around by some backway, you will get out of this in some way or other, and I will be just as much impeded by this as you will be. The man who has this right of passing under that state of affairs, sits back and says:	Well, I have nothing to
say, that is no affair of mine, I have no ground to stand upon. That individual in that position would consider he had no rights, no possible ground even of remonstrance or of expostulation, and that it was for him to sit there with his eyes blind to what was going on, trusting simply that when it was all done some sort of a passage would be given him. Now if we carry that out, if we were dealing with an individual, I am very much afraid that when the individual came later to complain, it would be said to him: You sat by and you saw all this done, and you made no complaint. True, you had a right, but you have acquiesced in all this, you have absolutely allowed the proprietor of these roads to go to great expense in making these obstructions, but you never said a word, you are too late now to complain. It seems to me that is precisely the position that is created by this government for Canada in connection with this matter. Now is the time, when these things are proposed, now is the time for us to come forward with the affirmation of our right to be consulted with regard to what is going to be done affecting navigation. When we are face to face with a prima facie obstruction affecting navigation, it is for us to insist that we have an opportunity of satisfying our-' Mr. DOHERTY.
selves that navigation is not going to be interfered with. Fortunately for us the Congress of the United States appears to have been more careful of our interests, at all events, their action would indicate a greater carefulness for our interests than seems to have existed in the minds of the government.
What seems to me is the key of this whole thing is the fact that we are not dealing with any mere general disposition giving equal rights in these boundary waters to both countries; but we are dealing with specific legislation to create a right affecting navigation in waters almost exclusively if not exclusively within the territory of the United States. Of course, I do not argue that if the United States proceeds absolutely to obstruct these channels, if they say they won't abide by the treaty, that we have any very effective method of securing our rights short of the last resort. But I do not think we should assume as towards these people that they have any deliberate desire to violate our rights in the matter, that they are not willing to hear us when we have such a manifest interest in this matter, and that they are not prepared to respect our rights if we put them properly before them. To do so would not only be most offensive to them, but if that is our frame of mind on the subject, why, it is a matter for surprise that we should so recently have made another treaty with them; because if we assume that they will be untrue to their obligations under the Ashburton Treaty, what reason have we to believe they will be true to their obligations under the recent Waterways Treaty? There is another thing I want to add. I think the argument of the Minister of Justice to the effect that our right under the Boundaries Treaty to have the commission pass upon the question of obstructions to be created in the future, is limited to cases where those obstructions affect the level of the water upon our side, is an additional argument showing the urgency of our intervening in this particular matter before the thing is carried out at all. Of course, I am not in a position to say whether what is proposed will or will not affect the level of the waters on our side of the St. Lawrence; but, if they do, . apparently we would have some right to have the matter submitted to the Boundary Commission. But if it merely interferes with navigation, then, as I read the recent treaty, and as I understand the Minister of Justice to read it, we will have no right to say that this matter must be submitted to the Boundary Waters Commission, because the section is perfectly clear that the consent of the Boundary Waters Commission is required only in cases where obstruction in the boundary water affects the level on the other side. That, as I understand it, is the argument of the Minister

of Justice as to the effect of section 3, and it seems to be only an additional argument making it clear that now, before this thing is carried out, is the time for Canada to make her voice heard.

As to the legal phase of this subject, I do not wish to say a word, simply because I do not consider myself icompetent to deal with it after it *has been dealt with by the two able legal gentlemen who have just spoken. I would like to say a word or two on the practical side of the question. I am sure it is a matter of considerable satisfaction to everybody in Canada who is opposed to the damming of the St. Lawrence under any circumstances that the United States Congress has thrown out the Bill. I am inclined to agree with the hon. member for South Sim-coe (Mr. Lennox) that this company will come forward again and endeavour to get authority both from the United States and from Canada to dam the St. Lawrence river. One reason why I am opposed to this damming of the St. Lawrence is that we could not now, or within the next five years, use our half of the power that would be generated. There is no question but that 500,000 horse-power could be generated there; in fact, some engineers put it as high as 800,000 horse-power. But, taking the smaller figure, if you had that power generated to-day you could not dispose of it in Canada at points near enough to the Long Sault for it to be used advantageously. A large amount of power is used in the city of Montreal. That power can be secured at points as close or closer than the Long Sault in streams not of an international character, and in places where it can be developed for far less money per horse-power than at the Long Sault.
And the hon. gentleman (Mr. Turriff) is right-the St. Lawrence is not international below Cornwall.

No, but it is

at that particular point. As I have said, you could not use in Canada our share of the power when generated. How, then, could you prevent it being sent to New York? It could be sold in New York at a high price, and that is where it would go ; and once it went there, we' would never get it back for use in. Canada. We have had our experience at Niagara, we have had our experience at Fort Frances ; why should we take any chances? I venture the assertion that, if that power is left alone, and if, latqr, the people of Canada decide that it is valuable enough to justify the injury to navigation, in fifty years from this time, the power of the Long Sault would be worth the amount of Canada's national debt to-day. If that be the case, why should we part with our right to any company, whether Canadian or
American?-but this company is practically altogether an American company.
Now, among the greatest objections raised to this scheme are those raised on behalf of the Richelieu and Ontario Navigation Company. I have it on what I consider the most absolute authority that this Aluminum Company of New York, who have been hoping to get the right to dam the St. Lawrence, have been and are-if the action of Congress in throwing out the Bill has not put an end to it-buying-up the stock of the Richelieu and Ontario Navigation Company in order to silence the objections that have been raised on behalf of that company. But I consider that this should not have any effect. What I would like to see would be something even more definite than the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) has given the House, although I think that what he has said must be fairly satisfactory-that is that nothing will be done in the way of approving of the plans for the damming of the St. Lawrence without fully consulting the House of Commons Urst. That is very satisfactory so far as it goes, but I would prefer that the government-should take the position that, for the present at all events-I suppose no government can decide what should be done in the future-absolutely nothing shall be done, and no company, Canadian, American, or any other, shall be allowed to dam the St. Lawrence for the purpose of producing power. I am satisfied that the power Is not needed, or, if it be needed, it can be got elsewhere, and got as cheaply, leaving the navigation of the St. Lawrence unaffected. I am glad to hear the discussion that has taken place, because I am satisfied that all we want to do is to have this matter aired in the House of Commons, and let the people of the Dominion, understand the exact position ; for if they* understand the exact position they will not allow the St. Lawrence to be dammed, and no government will dare allow it to be dammed.
Or they will be damned themselves.

Yes, as my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) says, they would be damned themselves. I am glad the American Congress has taken the sensible view and refused to pass the legislation asked for by the Aluminum Company ; -and I trust the government of Canada will do no less in the matter when the question is put up to them.

I am sure the House and the country are under deep obligation to the leader of the opposition for having brought this matter to the attention of the House to have it thoroughly discussed as it has been to-day. My hon. friend from Grenville (Mr. Reid)

brought uip the question of transmitting the power-even if this Long Sault dam were constructed-to Prescott and other towns in eastern Ontario, and stated that power could be transmitted to Prescott just as easily from Ottawa as 'from Cornwall. He also spoke of other towns in eastern Ontario being supplied from powers developed on the Trent canal. The government, I understand, have disposed of the powers there, and the company that has taken them over is looking over the field to arrange for disposing of the power when it is developed. I wish the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) were in his place, but as he is not here, I would suggest to the Prime Minister to discuss with that -hon. gentleman the question of this and other powers, and to have them examined by competent engineers. All the water that passes through the Long Sault passes down by the Thousand islands. On the Canadian side of the Thousand islands, at the Fiddler's elbow, owing to the islands there 'being so close together, we have a current of eight or ten miles an hour for some distance. My opinion is that, at far less expense, and without interfering with navigation, without raising the water at all. but merely by putting in a current wheel, an undershot wheel, as much power could be developed as at the Long Sault rapids. Such wheels could foe put in some of the narrow channels which are not used for navigation. We have another power in eastern Ontario that could supply many points. The government own and control the Rideau canal. Between Newboro, at the north end of my constituency, and Kingston, there is a total fall of about 200 feet-at Kingston Mills about 50 feet ; at Upper and Lower Brewers, 20 feet ; Jones' "Falls, 80 feet ; Fosters', 15 feet ; Chaffee's, 15 feet ; Bedford Mills, 20 feet. All these falls could be concentrated into one power. My hon. friend from Kingston (Mr. Harty) understands the situation, and I am satisfied will say a word in support of this suggestion. The effect of this improvement would be not merely to develop power but also to improve navigation. The navigation of the Rideau canal is practically spoiled because the waters are allowed to run away in the spring freshets. If the government wilt control the Bedford mills, owned by the Tett brothers, where the whole flow of water from Frontenac comes out, including the water from Bofob's lake and other lakes, a large power could be developed, and the water could foe prevented from running away in the spring. This could be reserved for navigation purposes, it would give the Rideau canal a full supply of water, and there would be a surplus with which to develop electrical power. I do not know how many hundreds of horse-power could be developed, but it would be a very large quantity. The hon. member for Kingston Mr. TAYLOR (Leeds).
(Mr. Harty) has gone into it more exhaustively than I have, but both of these powers could foe developed, in the one case, without interfering with navigation -and, in the other case, to the benefit of navigation. I would recommend to the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) that he would have both of these systems looked into and reserved for the benefit of the people of the eastern part of Ontario. We need not then go either to the Trent for a supply of power, or to the Ontario Electrical Power Commission, or to the Sault. We have powers in quantity to-day that are going to waste.

Before this motion is put, I wish to say a word about it. I am afraid, from the action of the government, as evidenced by the hon. Minister of Justice (Sir Allen Ayles-worth), that we are going to continue the same bad habit that we have had here for a good many years, of sitting complacently by waiting until the mischief is done, then regretting it and trying to regain some of the ground which we have lost. This dealing with the waters on the boundary between the United States and Canada has a history and a history which is not very creditable to the ingenuity of Canadians. In 1901 the United States woke up, or had awakened before that-at all events, they began to act with regard to the necessity of looking out for their own interests with regard to the water-powers to be derived; from international streams. Away back in 1901, ten years ago, the Congress of the United States appointed a committee to get all the evidence ready so as to be prepared to chloroform and bunco Canada, and in that they have succeeded pretty well. There is no use of talking about the Waterways Treaty being a good deal for Canada; it does not give to us a half, or a quarter, of what we ought to have had without any treaty or arrangement. The United States were awake and active ten years, ago, and the result was the appointment of a committee by Congress to take hold of the matter in the interests of the United States in order to quietly get the evidence, or at all events, to ascertain their rights and to strike at Canada for a treaty, when they were ready and when Canada would not be. They succeeded-there is no use in pretending that they did not- in getting the better of us as they always do when they deal with us. It is about time that the Minister of Justice or somebody else woke up to the necessity of acting ahead of time and not afterwards with regard to these encroachments by the United States upon our rights. When I heard of that committee being appointed in 1901 I had the temerity to put a question upon the Order Paper-the first ques-

tion that I ever asked in this House-as to whether this government had knowledge of the appointment of the committee by the Congress of the United States, and if so what they were going to do about getting their evidence ready to meet the arbitration that it was proposed to bring about. The right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) answered that he had heard nothing of it, that it was entirely unknown to him, that nothing to his knowledge had taken place in regard to it. Four or five years afterwards, and not until four or five years afterwards, the suggestion was made that these matters should be dealt with by what became known subsequently as the International Waterways Commission. I point this out because the officers of the United States had their evidence all ready when the inquiry came to be made. In the meantime they had had their surveyors through the county which I have the honour to represent and the adjoining county of Welland, making all sorts of surveys, ascertaining all the data they could, so that if they were confronted at the tribunal with any evidence from the Canadian standpoint that did not suit them they could contradict it, or, if it did suit them they could let it go. For four or five years their military surveyors were permitted to make surveys with regard to the Niagara river to ascertain how the power could be developed and where the boundary was, and they were ready to negotiate for the Waterways Treaty when the Waterways Commission was appointed and the treaty was made. I am not objecting to this having been done, but I am pointing out what was done. I say this because of what I think is the unfortunate carelessness, not to use the stronger word, of the Minister of Justice in talking about these matters. The other day he said that apparently there was no need of doing anything. To-day he practically says the same thing, but revises, not to say recants, the oponion he gave then as to the necessity the government are under of doing something. The Minister of Justice read us a lecture upon no nroposition and no necessity. That is why I said what I did- no proposition and no necessity of doing anything just at present! There will always be a necessity in Canada of being ready to meet incursions from the United States in regard to these assets, rights and resources of this great country. The Minister of Justice does not seem to be quite clear as to what he ought to do in the interest of Canada, but he complacently says that because Congress has turned down the proposition as at present made, and since he made his speech last week-not before-there is no need of any alarm. Then the Minister of Justice took a great deal of time to say that he had not meant
us to understand what he said, or meant to say, in his speech on February 2, as we did understand it. The hon. gentleman, in the course of his statement in justification of what he said he meant to say on February 2, read a paragraph from the middle of page 2969 of ' Hansard.' The middle paragraph that he read is on ' Hansard,' but perhaps, on reflection I should read it in order to get the connection with what I desire to say. He read:
That is exactly the situation under the existing treaties. The right of navigation is paramount and that right is secured. That right exists in this United States channel which it is proposed to dam, just as it exists in the old Channel between Sheik island and the mainland of Ontario, which is to-day utilized as part of our Cornwall canal. The right of navigation is secured by treaty and is not proposed to be interfered with. On the contrary, it is proposed to be helped according to the plans of the promoters, and unless the right of navigation is interfered with, or the level altered on our own side, we have under existing treaties, no cause to object.
That is what the Minister of Justicq read to-day as justifying his opinion that as long s navigation was not .interfered with we in Canada could not object. But the hon. gentleman said something more immediately following that, and that is what I am going to read. He went on and said:	-jf f
I do not think much is to he gained by going back to the terms of the Ashburton Treaty because we have a new treaty on this very subject which goes further, which governs this very situation, and which has been ratified by both countries and is in force today. Under the provisions of that treaty, while it prohibits the construction of any obstructions in boundary waters except under certain circumstances, it impliedly gives permission to obstruct boundary waters.
In view of that statement, how can any hon. gentlemen on this side of the House be blamed for believing that the Minister ' of Justice was justifying this obstruction? Why should the Minister of Justice mention and reiterate everything that it would be possible to reiterate and suggest on behalf of the United States in attempting to usurp or take away from us those privileges? It is exactly as if we on this side of the House were representing Canada and the other side of the House the United States, and as if the Minister of Justice were presenting the United States argument. No counsel for the United States could put it stronger if he were contending that Canada had no right to object. Why should our Minister of Justice seek for ways and means and arguments to sustain any claim the United States might make, that we could not assert our rights on the St. Lawrence. The Minister of Justice spoke about the absence of a treaty, but

what is the waterways agreement if it is not a treaty? He told us that under Article 3 of the Waterways Treaty we could not prevent the Americans doing this if it did not affect the natural level or flow of boundary waters on either side of the line. But Article 3 must be consistently read with Articles 4, 8, 9 and 10 of the same treaty, and Article 4 reads:
The high contracting parties agree that, except in cases provided for by special agreement between them, they will not permit the construction or maintenance on their respective sides of the boundary of any remedial or protective works or any dams or other obstructions in waters flowing from boundary waters or in waters at a lower level than the boundary in rivers flowing across the boundary, the effect of which is to raise the natural level of waters on the other side of the boundary unless the construction or maintenance thereof is approved by the aforesaid International Joint Commission.
It is further agreed that the waters herein defined as boundary waters and waters flowing across the boundary shall not be polluted on either side to the injury of health or property on the other side.
Mark you, that applies not to one country, but to both. Neither is to permit any remedial or protective works, or any dams or other constructions in waters flowing from boundary waters, or in waters flowing from a lower level. But the Minister of Justice undertakes to assume that article 3 is to be read as if article 4 was not there at all, and to construe it that it is only to apply if the level of the water is lowered. Then article 8 reads in part:
The high contracting parties shall have, each on its own side of the boundary, equal and similar rights in the use of the waters hereinbefore defined as boundary waters.
The following order of precedence shall be observed among the various uses enumerated hereinafter for these waters and no use shall be permitted which tends materially to conflict with or restrain any other use which is given preference over it in this order of precedence:
1.	Uses for domestic and sanitary purposes.
2.	Uses for navigation, including the service of canals for the purposes of navigation.
3.	Uses for power and for irrigation purposes.
I pause there to interject that the Joint International Commission undertake to lay down principles which have been adopted in the treaty, and which are supposed to govern both countries in this matter. That is for the future; that is to apply to matters arising, such as this, after the treaty was signed. First, absolute precedence is given to the uses of these waters for domestic and sanitary purposes. Has the Minister of Justice inquired whether this work would have had a prejudicial effect in relation to sanitary or domestic purposes. He assumes it has not, but, if he is not Mr. LANCASTER.
counsel for the United States, then in the interests of Canada he should undertake such an inquiry. Then the second preference is given to uses for navigation, including the service of canals for the purpose of navigation, and, in the third place, to uses for power and irrigation purposes. The article goes on to say:
The foregoing provisions shall not apply to or disturb any existing uses of boundary waters on either side of the boundary.
The requirements for an equal division may in the discretion of the commission be suspended in cases of temporary diversions along boundary waters at points where such equal division cannot be made advantageously on account of local conditions, and where such diversion does not diminish elsewhere the amount available for use on the other side.
The commission in its discretion may make its approval in any case conditional upon the construction of remedial or protective works to compensate so far as possible for the particular use or diversion proposed, and in such cases may require that suitable and adequate provision, approved by the commission, be made for the protection and indemnity against injury of any interests on either side of the boundary.
Then comes article 9, which provides:
The high contracting parties further agree that any other question or matter of difference arising between them involving the rights, obligations or interests of either in relation to the other or to the inhabitants of the other, along the common frontier between the United States and the Dominion of Canada, shall be referred from time to time to the International Joint Commission for examination and report, whenever either the government of the United States or the government of the Dominion of Canada shall request that such questions or matters of difference be so referred.
Does not the Minister of Justice think this is one of the matters of difference that ought to be so referred. Look at the responsibility which the treaty throws upon both governments ; look at the language of it for the protection of both parties. I ask, should not the Minister of Justice have done more than used his energy and ability to discuss the dictionary meaning of ' equally free and open?' Should he not use all his ingenuity to protect the rights^ of Canada, instead of endeavouring to point out that certain language in the Ashburton Treaty is not what it was supposed by the rest of us to be? In view of the fact that certain United States citizens have actually gone to Congress for power to interfere with the rights of the people of Canada, why did not the Minister of Justice submit to the International Waterways Commission that there was a difference such as is provided for in the treaty, and prepare a case for Canada, and submit it to this tribunal, which is supposed to be independent, and then we on this side of the House would not, from day to day, be compelled to apply to the

government to check these incursions by the United States upon the rights of our country. But what the Minister of Justice seemed to do was to throw out the hint to the United States that if they made the contention we were afraid they would make so far as he is concerned he would agree with them.
What greater invitation could there be to the United States to take everything they can get from us in this connection, than the knowledge that the first law officer of the Crown in the Dominion of Canada, ahead of time, has said that in his opinion they have these rights, and we cannot prevent them from exercising them if they choose to do so? The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff), I think quite properly, complimented the United States Congress upon turning down this charter; but I could not help noticing that he did not say a word about the Minister of Justice. He evidently thought that the Minister of Justice belonged to the other side, and was entitled to be condemned, because, by his speech of last week, he practically invited Congress to take what they could. But Congress, perhaps out of sympathy for Canada, not wishing to take too much from her all at once, showed a good deal more desire to protect Canada than the Minister of Justice evidences. The hon. member for Assiniboia referred to our experience on the Niagara river, where we got the worst of it in all these matters. As I demonstrated years before this treaty was negotiated, they were entitled, according to the boundary line, to one-tenth of the power, while this commission gave them more than four-tenths. They woke up years before we did and began to help themselves, and when we woke up it was too late to get full justice. As the hon. member for Assiniboia said, it will be the same in this case: we shall get about one-half of what we should have, while the United States will get two or three times what it should have. There is a way provided by the treaty in which this matter can be dealt with, and in order to show what powers this government possess, if they like to use them, I want to read a few words of Article X.
Any question or matters of difference arising between the high contracting parties involving the rights, obligations, or interests of the United States or of the Dominion of Canada either in relation to each other or to their respective inhabitants, may be referred for decision to the International Joint Commission by the consent of the two parties.
This government could ask the United States government to consent to have this matter adjusted. Now, Sir, I would urge upon the Prime Minister that he ought to see that his Minister of Justice takes a different position to what he has done on these matters. The Minister of Justice ought all the time to hold a brief for Canada. He
ought to be the keenest man in the whole country to suspect that these people are trying to make incursions upon us which they are not entitled to make. He does not seem to hold even a watching brief for Canada, but he stands up here and give3 the United States to understand that we cannot stop them. The Prime Minister should direct his Minister of Justice to make his complaint, and see that the Waterways Commission takes hold of this matter and settles it properly, instead of trifling with the House, as he has done to-day, by taking the ground that equally free and open navigation does not mean that both parties are to have free and open navigation, but means that we are not to have it if the other party does not want it. I protest against the apathy of the government in these matters, and I hope they will turn over a new leaf and be more alert to protect us, and not wait again until the horse is stolen before they lock the stable door.
Motion agreed to.

Before the orders of the day are called, I see a reference in the papers to a telegram said to have been sent by the Minister of Finance to the High Commissioner in London with reference to the reciprocity arrangement made with the United States. I would like to ask the minister if he would be kind enough to lay a copy of that telegram on the table of the House before to-morrow.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think it is given correctly in the evening paper; but if I find any inaccuracy in it, I will send a copy in correct form to the hon. gentleman.

I would like also to suggest that the papers on the Farmers' Bank, No. 110B and HOC, which take in the curator's report and the correspondence brought down by the Minister of Finance, be printed, and that the rule of the House be suspended for that purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
They are largely such formalities that I hardly thought it necessary, but I have no objection to the hon. gentleman's motion.

Mr. VERVILLE moved the third reading of Bill (No. 3) respecting the hours of labour on public works.

This Bill was discussed last week in my absence. I was a member of the committee to which it was referred. Everything was done to secure evidence, I have no fault to find on that score, but I am opposed to the Bill for the simple reason that it is discriminating. I do not know why we should provide for an eight hour day for men working on public buildings when men working on other buildings have to work ten hours. I believe the Bill, if it is made law, will cause trouble. I have had a great deal of experience with help for years. My experience extends over thirty years, and the complaint with us has been that we do not give them sufficient work. For that reason I wish to put myself on record as being opposed to the Bill, believing as I do, after hearing the evidence, that it will cause trouble.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
As a member of the special committee who heard the evidence last year, I desire to say a word. My objection to the Bill is not very strong as I am in favour of helping on the eight-hour movement and the labouring people, but I wish to place on record a communication which I have received from Moncton. It is as follows:
Moncton, N.B., December 28, 1910. John Stanfield, Esq., M.P.,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-We, the undersigned, representing organized labour in the city of Moncton, hereby enter an emphatic protest against the proposed amendments to the Eight-Hour Bill (known as Bill No. 3), which amendments, if passed, will utterly eliminate from its benefits the thousands of employees of the government on the Intercolonial and Prince Edward Island railways. We particularly object to the striking out of section 5 of the Bill.
We believe that in the matter of hours and wages and in ideal working conditions generally the government of the country should be the leader, not the follower. To this end we would urgently request your support to the Bill as originally proposed.
Thanking you in advance for any support you can render us at this time.
We remain, yours very truly,
